project_tracker_diagnostic: Biennial/perennial native thistle with pink-purple discoid heads; leaves armed with relatively narrow marginal spines; common in pastures and roadsides across much of Texas.

project_inclusion.learning_reason: Common, conspicuous, or high-value comparison species for Central Texas field ID.

morphology_keys.habit: Erect thistle, usually under about 1 m.
morphology_keys.leaves: Middle/upper sessile leaves may have broad clasping auricles AND may extend as spiny decurrent wings. Image confirmation requires attachment on the same stem. The upper leaf surface is thinly cobwebby/tomentose, lower face densely white-woolly; C. vulgare has diagnostic stiff short spines on the upper blade.
morphology_keys.heads: Purple to pink discoid heads, solitary or in small groups; no ray florets.
morphology_keys.phyllaries: Involucre around 12–20 mm high (FNA key and UT Austin detailed Texas treatment). Outer/middle phyllaries often carry a narrow whitish, sticky, glutinous medial ridge; UT Austin describes ~2.5–4 mm ridge on sampled phyllaries. A visible pale line need not be sticky in every photo and is not exclusive among Cirsium.
best_field_traits: spiny but not extremely woolly foliage
morphology_keys.stem: UT Austin Williamson flora documents ridged, somewhat winged stems on robust Texas thistle, with about two spinescent decurrent wings from each cauline leaf. This OVERLAPS winged C. vulgare; do not use a winged/not-winged rule.

photo_strategy.selection_logic: Prefer curated taxon photos plus multiple views from one Central Texas/Texas observation.

look_here_first: FIRST measure the green involucre UNDER the flower heads (excluding florets and projecting phyllary spines): local Texas thistle specimen descriptions give roughly 15–20 mm in height. SECOND examine a stem LEAF NODE: the broad sessile upper leaf may make small spine-tipped clasping ears (auricles) and CAN continue as DECURRENT, SPINY STEM WINGS on robust plants. Do not assume wings mean introduced C. vulgare! Instead compare bull thistle's short bristle-spines emerging on the UPPER leaf blade. Check whitish glutinous longitudinal phyllary midridges where visible. C. horridulum has markedly larger 40–45 mm involucres in Williamson County specimens, largely hidden by a separate ring of spinescent upper leaves.

comparisons.key_distinctions: C. horridulum has the extra under-head collar of very spinescent upper leaves and a much larger involucre (~40–45 mm in UT Williamson description) compared with C. texanum's ~15–20 mm. C. texanum upper stem leaf bases can clasp with auricles OR descend as spiny wings on robust plants; C. vulgare also has wings but distinctive short bristle-spines on upper LEAF FACE. Do not teach winged/not-winged as an absolute species split.
